What are the key GCP services you have u: Group by category with honest depth per service - Compute (GKE, Compute Engine), Storage (Cloud Storage, Persistent Disk), Networking (VPC, Cloud Load Balancing), Data (Cloud SQL, BigQuery), and Operations (Cloud Monitoring/Logging) - rather than a flat list implying equal expertise across everything.
What is the difference between GKE Stand: Standard mode gives full control over node configuration - you manage node pools, machine types, and node-level settings yourself, paying for provisioned node capacity regardless of utilization. Autopilot mode abstracts nodes away entirely - GKE manages node provisioning/sizing automatically based on your workloads' actual resource requests, and you're billed per-Pod resource usage rather than per-node, trading some control (no direct node access, more restricted workload configurations) for significantly less operational overhead.
Can you explain the GKE architecture?: The control plane (API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd) is fully managed by Google. Node pools (in Standard mode) are worker VMs you configure, running kubelet, kube-proxy, and a container runtime - kubelet manages Pod lifecycle on that node and reports status back to the control plane through the API server, which is the single point of interaction between all components and the cluster's stored state.
How do you secure a GKE cluster?: Use private clusters (nodes without public IPs), Workload Identity instead of downloaded service account keys, least-privilege IAM for both cluster access and workload service accounts, Binary Authorization to enforce only signed/scanned images can deploy, NetworkPolicies for Pod-to-Pod traffic restriction, and regular node/control-plane version upgrades to stay patched against known CVEs - layering these rather than relying on any single control.
Have you used Jenkins CI/CD pipelines wi: Answer honestly with specifics - the integration mechanism used (Bitbucket webhook triggering Jenkins, or the Bitbucket Branch Source plugin for multibranch pipelines) and one concrete pipeline you built/maintained with that integration.
What is the CI workflow in Jenkins?: A commit/PR triggers a webhook to Jenkins, which runs the Jenkinsfile's defined stages - checkout, build, unit test, static analysis/security scan - reporting status back to the source control platform (a green/red check on the PR) - failing fast at the earliest stage that catches an issue rather than running all stages regardless.
How would you design a CI/CD pipeline in: Cloud Build (or Jenkins/GitHub Actions) triggers on a commit to the source repo, runs build/test/security-scan steps, builds a container image and pushes it to Artifact Registry tagged with the commit SHA, then deploys to GKE (via kubectl/Helm from the pipeline, or via ArgoCD watching a GitOps manifests repo) - progressing through dev/staging with automated tests, then production behind a manual approval or automated canary analysis gate, with automatic rollback if post-deploy health checks fail.
Would you use Cloud Source Repositories: External repositories (GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket) are far more common in practice for their richer collaboration features (PR reviews, branch protection UI, broader plugin/integration ecosystem) - Cloud Source Repositories is mainly useful as a mirror for private/air-gapped scenarios or tight native integration with other GCP services, but most teams default to an external Git platform and integrate it with GCP's build/deploy tooling via webhooks or triggers.

How do you monitor containerized applica: Layer infrastructure metrics (Pod/node CPU, memory, restart counts via Prometheus/Cloud Monitoring) with application-level metrics (request rate, error rate, latency exposed via a `/metrics` endpoint) and centralized logging (stdout/stderr shipped to Cloud Logging/ELK, since container filesystems are ephemeral) - the combination is what gives full visibility, since infrastructure metrics alone won't reveal an application-level bug.
How do you perform logging and troublesh: For Docker: `docker logs <container>` (and `--previous` equivalent isn't native to Docker but `docker logs` on a restarted container still shows prior output until restart). For Kubernetes: `kubectl logs <pod>` and `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` for a crashed container's last output before restart, combined with `kubectl describe pod` for scheduling/lifecycle events - centralized log aggregation (Cloud Logging, ELK) is essential in production since `kubectl logs` only works while the Pod still exists.
Which monitoring tools have you used for: Name the actual tools and the specific role each played - Prometheus/Cloud Monitoring for metrics and alerting, ELK or Cloud Logging for centralized logs, Datadog if used as a unified commercial alternative - and one concrete dashboard or alert you built/tuned, since depth on actual usage matters more than the breadth of tools named.
